arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Mr. Pincus argued the exhaustion doctrine terminates all patent rights after an authorized sale. He cited the Bowman case to support this broad interpretation.
Mr. Stewart addressed the domestic exhaustion issue first. He responded to questions about why the doctrine lacks codification.
Mr. Trela agreed with the government on one point. He stated the Federal Circuit properly looked to the statute for the doctrine's limits.
Justice Alito questioned the strategy of disregarding a rule adopted by the Federal Circuit. He noted this approach seemed counterintuitive for patent holders.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: The case tests the patent exhaustion doctrine. This doctrine limits patent rights after an authorized sale. The core dispute involves sales made outside the United States.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: Impressions wants the Court to hold that a foreign authorized sale exhausts U.S. patent rights. This would allow the resale of imported goods without infringement liability.
Lexmark wants the Court to hold that a foreign sale does not exhaust U.S. patent rights. This would allow patent holders to enforce use restrictions on imported goods.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: Impressions argues the exhaustion doctrine applies regardless of where the sale occurs. They contend the initial authorized sale terminates all patent rights to that specific item.
Lexmark argues the exhaustion doctrine is limited by statute. They contend the patent holder retains the right to restrict use of items sold under foreign laws.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: This case defines the geographic scope of patent exhaustion. It determines whether patent holders can control the resale of goods sold abroad. The outcome affects the global trade of patented products. It shapes the balance between patent rights and free commerce.
